title: Public Knowledge, Private Returns
subtitle: Broadly Speaking, The Store Got Nicer, Everyone Loves a Curve (Until They’re Under It), You Can Lose it All (Just Not Like That), Nineteen For One
body_html:
Broadly Speaking

It is a remarkably durable trend that market capitalizations distribute as a power law. Investment strategies nominally dedicated to “diversification” are, therefore, liable to be massively concentrated. In recent decades, this concentration has intensified on a second axis: industry. In the 1980s, the ten largest names spanned industrials, energy, automotives, and telecommunications. Today, the majority are in information technology.

This has occurred alongside an increase in the first concentration axis, as well. In 2015, the Magnificent 7 represented 12% of the S&P 500 by market capitalization. Today, that proportion is closer to 35%.1 Last year (2025) 40% of the S&P 500’s return was attributable to these 7 companies, and that proportion was more than 50% in the two prior years23.

The upshot? Over the past 10 years, “owning the market” has been a narrow bet on information technology.

The Store Got Nicer

A side-effect of these same leaps in information technology has been the ability for retail investors (and otherwise) to avoid the historically characteristic phone calls with brokers, manual rebalancing of portfolios and reinvestment of dividends, payment of hefty commission fees, and forced use of clunky, disaggregated research tools in favor of commissionless, fractional, and real-time investment tools. All in one’s pocket.

Everyone Loves a Curve (Until They’re Under It)

For the past few decades, this was enough. Ordinary people were able to buy a share of Microsoft when the company was generating $197m in revenue4, Amazon at $16m5, and Facebook at $3.7B6. Figures dwarfed by their modern counterparts.

But things are changing.

Anthropic, next in line to join these names, is valued at over $1T, a valuation that Microsoft reached 33 years7 AFTER going public. Facebook and Amazon? 218 and 99 years, respectively. The curve is getting steeper.

Why is this?

Any single explanation would be overdetermined. Perhaps Anthropic and the handful of other frontier labs (OpenAI, namely) with similar revenue and valuation growth profiles simply haven’t had the time to go public. But the role of private funding seems operative here.

In the late 1990s, VCs held $143B in AUM10. Today, that figure is $1.25T11. Frontier labs, with their own curves, have enormous capital requirements that used to be satisfied only through an IPO. Now these needs can be met by a late-stage fundraising ecosystem. All with fewer relationships to manage, lower regulatory costs, and fewer reporting requirements.

Anthropic’s series H round raised $65B12. Two months prior, OpenAI raised $122B13. These amounts dwarf every IPO in recorded history- SpaceX’s recent IPO excepted.

You Can Lose it All (Just Not Like That)

For most of history, the curve was largely public. But this has changed. Retail was forced to hold its breath as Anthropic’s ARR grew by a factor of ten for each of the past three years.14

Observe an inconsistency: anyone can interact with models mere months behind the frontier and listen to industry leaders discuss them. But investing activity in the the frontier labs is restricted to accredited investors and institutional players, along with insiders.

The consequence of this is that the typical American can buy a lottery ticket or bet on the likelihood of Jesus returning by year-end, but cannot purchase an ownership interest in Anthropic.

That capital is distributed unequally throughout the population- much like market capitalizations themselves- isn’t an injustice to be remedied. What is an injustice, however, is artificially bounding the universe of participants in a market under the guise of protection against information asymmetries and illiquidity.

Nineteen for One

For retail investors looking for solutions:

Some large technology companies have made prescient investments in the frontier labs. Buying Google provides indirect, diluted exposure to Anthropic: a 14% stake worth $135B value on a $3B investment15. Nearly half of Google’s Q1 2026 profit came from marking up its stake in Anthropic16. Likewise, buying Microsoft has a 27% /$228B stake in OpenAI from a $13B investment17.

A handful of tender offering and interval funds, like USVC18 and ARKVX19 sell ownership interests in a basket of private companies- including Anthropic and OpenAI- to retail, priced at NAV. These funds have liquidity implications through redemption caps or otherwise.

Then there’s VCX, a closed-end fund including a ~20% allocation for Anthropic. At its peak, it traded at 19x premium to NAV (~5x at the time of writing).20 Prototypical low float dynamics.

There are also perpetual futures: leveraged synthetic positions enabling long/short trading in private companies against a variable interest rate tied to the difference between instrument and underlying. Various markets, most notably Hyperliquid, have offered “perps” for Anthropic and OpenAI. However, these qualify as single security swaps and are therefore non-compliant with SEC requirements. Hyperliquid is not registered with the SEC and explicitly prohibits Americans from trading.21 It recently shut down its “Ventuals” program, which included perpetual futures for Anthropic and OpenAI.22

At the risk of stating the obvious, the above set of “solutions” for retail money is lacking. These are the largest private companies in the US by an order of magnitude. That they’ve chosen to remain private at this scale, rather than go public is not a failing of them, but public market infrastructure and policy to adapt to a matured risk capital ecosystem.

The money will be raised, risk taken, prices discovered, and fortunes made. The questions are about who is allowed to play and when.

Notes:

  • On Private/Public funding dynamics:

    • The JOBS Act moving the maximum number of private company shareholders from 500 to 2,000 (excluding employees) also contributed to the trend of private companies delaying going public for longer.

  • On Perpetual Futures

    • At peak, the Ventuals program had a peak volume of $650M between the Anthropic and OpenAI perps. Valuations of 1.62T and $1.34T for Anthropic and OpenAI, respectively.

  • On Retail “Missing Out”

    • The future is uncertain. Anthropic’s ARR growth trend may persist- Hume be damned- or not. The contention is not about any given investment. They may fail or succeed; it’s about retail money’s ability to participate in markets.
